verdict.rationale: Across Isaiah 53, the ransom sayings of Mark 10:45 and Matthew 20:28, Romans 3:25, 2 Corinthians 5:21, 1 Peter 2:24, 1 Peter 3:18, and 1 John 2:2 the same substitution vocabulary recurs without lexical contradiction. Isaiah 53 stacks the sin-bearing verbs "bear" (nasa, verses 4 and 12), "carry" (sabal, verses 4 and 11), and "cause to land on" (paga in the hiphil, the Hebrew causative form meaning 'to cause to do'). The LORD (Yahweh) causes the iniquity of us all to land on him (verse 6), and he intercedes for transgressors (verse 12). The first-person plural suffixes (the 'our' endings) name the speakers as the source of the load and the Servant as the one carrying it, and verse 10 calls his life a "guilt offering" (asham), the Levitical sacrifice. The New Testament reuses this engine: "a ransom in place of many" (lytron anti pollon), where "in place of" (anti) is the strongest substitution preposition, attested across the canon overwhelmingly in the sense in place of or instead of; "on behalf of us" (hyper hemon) and the "righteous on behalf of the unrighteous" (dikaios hyper adikon) construction; "to offer up" (anaphero, the Greek Old Testament, the Septuagint or LXX, verb for offering up) with our sins as object on the tree; and "place of atonement" (hilasterion) and "means of atonement" (hilasmos) as the cultic locus where sin is dealt with. The verdict holds without dependence on disputed variant readings.

scripture.force: First-person plural pronominal suffixes (the 'our' endings: "our sicknesses" cholayenu, and "our pains" makovenu) name the burden, and the verbs "bear" (nasa) and "carry" (sabal) predicate a transfer of that burden onto the third-person singular subject "he" (hu), the Servant. The grammar predicates substitutive load-bearing rather than parallel suffering.

The Pual participles (passive intensive forms) "pierced" (mecholal) and "crushed" (medukka) attach via the prepositional phrases "because of our transgressions" (mippeshaenu) and "because of our iniquities" (meawonotenu), grammatically marking the speakers as the cause of his wounding. The construction "the discipline of our peace was upon him" (musar shelomenu alav) places the chastisement formally on him while the peace accrues to us, and "by his wound there is healing for us" (ubachaburato nirpa lanu) makes his stripe the means of our healing. The verse predicates a one-for-another exchange.

The hiphil (the Hebrew causative form meaning 'to cause to do') "caused to land on" (hifgia of paga) with the LORD (Yahweh) as subject, "on him" (bo) as locus, and "the iniquity of us all" (et awon kullanu) as object predicates the LORD (Yahweh) causing the iniquity of all of us to strike or land on the Servant. The causative stem with the divine subject names the agent of the transfer, framing the iniquity itself as the thing transferred.

The clause "when his soul is made an asham" (im tasim asham nafsho, "asham" being the guilt offering) labels the Servant's life with "guilt offering" (asham), the technical Levitical term for the guilt or reparation offering. "Guilt offering" (asham) occurs 41 times in the canon and is concentrated in Leviticus 5 to 7, the guilt-offering legislation. Applying that cultic term to the Servant imports the sacrificial substitution structure: a guilt offering bears liability so the offerer goes free.

The clause "and he shall bear their iniquities" (waawonotam hu yisbol) repeats "carry" (sabal), the carry verb of verse 4, but now with "iniquities" (awonot) as the explicit object rather than sicknesses. The sin-bearing predication is therefore not confined to verses 4 to 6 but recurs in the closing summary of the Song, with iniquity itself as what the Servant carries.

The closing verse repeats "bear" (nasa) in "and he bore the sin of many" (wehu chet rabbim nasa) and "caused to land on" (paga) in "and he interceded or made contact on behalf of transgressors" (welapposhim yafgia). Both sin-bearing verbs of verses 4 and 6 return at the climax, with "many" (rabbim) as the beneficiaries, the same quantifier behind "a ransom in place of many" (lytron anti pollon) in the gospels. The bearing pattern brackets the whole Song.

The phrase "to give his life a ransom in place of many" (dounai ten psychen autou lytron anti pollon) joins "ransom" (lytron, the ransom price) to the preposition "in place of" (anti). Across its 20 attestations in the canon "in place of" (anti) carries the sense in place of or instead of as its dominant force (for example reigning in place of Herod in Matthew 2:22, eye for eye in Matthew 5:38, evil for evil in 1 Peter 3:9). With a personal object ("many," pollon) and a price noun, "in place of" (anti) is the strongest single-word marker of substitution in the New Testament, and "ransom" (lytron) is a New Testament noun limited to this saying and its parallel.

The Matthean parallel preserves "a ransom in place of many" (lytron anti pollon) verbatim. The repetition of the same "ransom" (lytron) plus "in place of" (anti) construction in a second gospel confirms the substitution reading is not an isolated phrasing but a fixed saying, and the noun "ransom" (lytron) occurs in the canon only here and at Mark 10:45.

"He bore up" (anenenken, aorist, a completed past action, of anaphero, the verb the Greek Old Testament, the Septuagint or LXX, uses for offering up sacrifices) takes "our sins" (tas hamartias hemon) as object and "in his body" (en to somati autou) plus "on the tree" (epi to xylon) as the place of bearing. The "so that" clause (hina-clause) "so that, having died to sins, we might live to righteousness" (apogenomenoi tais hamartiais te dikaiosyne zesomen) names the intended effect. The instrumental dative (the 'by-means-of' grammatical form) "by his wound you were healed" (to molopi autou iathete), echoing Isaiah 53:5, makes his stripe the means of the addressees healing. "To offer up" (anaphero) occurs only 10 times in the canon, weighted toward cultic offering language.

"Christ suffered once for sins, the righteous one for the unrighteous" (Christos hapax peri hamartion epathen, dikaios hyper adikon; "hapax" meaning a word or event that occurs only once). The contrast "righteous" (dikaios) over against "unrighteous" (adikon), joined by "on behalf of" (hyper) plus the genitive of persons (the 'of-persons' grammatical form), sets one party suffering on behalf of the opposite party. The pairing of an explicit righteous-for-unrighteous antithesis with a sin-suffering predicate states representative substitution in its plainest grammatical form.

"The one who knew no sin he made sin on our behalf" (ton me gnonta hamartian hyper hemon hamartian epoiesen) uses "on behalf of us" (hyper hemon) with the Father as the acting subject on the Son. The "so that" clause (hina-clause) "so that we might become the righteousness of God in him" (hina hemeis genometha dikaiosyne theou en auto) sets up an exchange: he becomes "sin" (hamartia) on our behalf, we become "righteousness" (dikaiosyne) in him. "On behalf of" (hyper) with a genitive of persons (the 'of-persons' grammatical form) plus a sin-bearing predicate names representative substitution.

"Whom God set forth as a place of atonement through faith in his blood" (hon proetheto ho theos hilasterion dia pisteos en to autou haimati). "Place of atonement" (hilasterion) occurs only twice in the canon, the other being Hebrews 9:5 of the "mercy seat" (kapporet) where atoning blood was applied. Pairing "place of atonement" (hilasterion) with "in his own blood" (en to autou haimati) ties that cultic locus to the Servant's own death. "The passing-over of previously committed sins" (paresin ton progegonoton hamartematon) and "for a demonstration of his righteousness" (eis endeixin tes dikaiosynes autou) frame the death as God's righteous resolution of previously unpunished sin.

"He himself is a means of atonement concerning our sins" (autos hilasmos estin peri ton hamartion hemon). "Means of atonement" (hilasmos) occurs only twice in the canon, both in this letter (here and 4:10), and in the Greek Bible denotes the means by which sin is dealt with in cultic context. The "concerning" phrase (peri-phrase) plus "sins" (hamartion) locates sin as what the "means of atonement" (hilasmos) addresses, with "he himself" (autos) predicating the Son himself as that means.

"Having disarmed the rulers and authorities he made a public spectacle of them, triumphing over them" (apekdysamenos tas archas kai tas exousias edeigmatisen en parresia, thriambeusas autous). "Triumph over" (thriambeuo, lead in triumph) frames the cross as victory over hostile powers rather than as load-bearing. The vocabulary here is military and triumphal, not sacrificial, which is why this verse anchors a victory model of the cross that the substitution terms do not cover. It does not deny substitution but it is not stated in substitution words.

"Christ suffered for you, leaving you a writing pattern to trace" (Christos epathen hyper hymon, hymin hypolimpanon hypogrammon). "Writing pattern" (hypogrammos, a writing copy for a pupil to trace) occurs only here in the canon and frames the suffering as an example to imitate. Standing three verses before the bearing language of 2:24, it shows the same author can describe the cross as pattern as well as substitution. The "writing pattern" (hypogrammos) word names an exemplary function the substitution terms do not, so it anchors an example model sitting alongside the bearing model.

complicating_texts.resolution: "Concerning the whole world" (peri holou tou kosmou) appears alongside "concerning ours" (peri ton hemeteron), which some read as undercutting a strictly definite substitution. Lexically, "means of atonement" (hilasmos) with a "concerning" plus genitive (peri-genitive) specifies the domain the "means of atonement" (hilasmos) addresses without by itself predicating equal application to every individual. The substitutionary-bearing predication is unaffected; the extent question is a separate lexical question the words here do not settle, not a defeater of the bearing pattern.

Matthew 8:17 applies Isaiah 53:4 to physical healings, which could suggest a non-penal reading of the verse in isolation. Lexically, "bear" (nasa) and "carry" (sabal) in Isaiah 53 take a chain of objects across verses 4 to 6, 11, and 12 that includes both "our sicknesses" (cholayenu) and "our pains" (makovenu, verse 4) AND "iniquities" (awonot), "transgression" (pesha), and "sin" (chet, verses 5 to 6, 11, 12). The same verbs operate over both sickness and iniquity; the Matthean citation foregrounds one object set without removing iniquity from the verbs grammar.

"Place of atonement" (hilasterion) has been read both as expiation (sin-covering) and propitiation (wrath-absorbing). The Pauline grammar pairs "place of atonement" (hilasterion) with "a demonstration of his righteousness" (endeixis tes dikaiosynes autou) and with "passing-over" (paresis) of previously unpunished sins, which presses toward a sense that includes the satisfaction of God's righteous response, not expiation alone. Either reading still predicates Christ as the cultic locus where sin is dealt with through his blood, so the substitutionary-bearing claim stands under both.

"Triumph over" (thriambeuo) frames the cross as triumph over the powers, a victory model stated in military rather than sacrificial vocabulary. This is a genuine second canonical pattern, not a contradiction. The substitution words ("in place of" anti, "on behalf of" hyper, the bearing verbs, "guilt offering" asham, "place of atonement" hilasterion) and the victory word ("triumph over" thriambeuo) both stand in the canon; the text does not rank the two models against each other. The proposition asserts the substitution model is true, which the bearing vocabulary supports, but the canon also frames the same death as conquest, so divergence among readers is over which model is central, not over whether substitution words are present.

"Writing pattern" (hypogrammos, a writing pattern to be traced) frames the suffering as an example to imitate, an exemplary model. It is not exhausted by the bearing language and the bearing language is not exhausted by it. The same author moves from example (verse 21) to bearing (verse 24) within one paragraph, so the example reading must sit alongside, rather than replace, the substitution reading. As with the victory model, the words attest both functions without ordering them.

variant_units_examined.note: Some witnesses vary the article before "faith" (pisteos), with no impact on the substitutionary predication: "place of atonement in his own blood" (hilasterion en to autou haimati) remains intact under either reading.
Singular versus plural variation on "wound" (molopi, his wound, or his wounds) does not affect the instrumental dative (the 'by-means-of' grammatical form) or the healing-by-his-stripe predication.
Article placement variants around "the one who knew no" (ton me gnonta) do not affect the "on behalf of us" (hyper hemon) construction or the "we might become" (genometha) exchange grammar.

The "ransom in place of many" (lytron anti pollon) clause is firmly attested across the witnesses; the Matthean parallel at 20:28 preserves the same wording, so the substitution reading does not hang on a single disputed text.

variants.note: The ECM apparatus (the critical edition of New Testament textual variants) editions do not cover Isaiah, the Synoptic gospels, Romans, 2 Corinthians, or 1 Peter at this writing, and the bundle reports not_in_ecm_scope true. Variant assessment relies on the standard apparatus; no variant materially affects the verdict.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Takes the bearing verbs "bear" (nasa), "carry" (sabal), "caused to land on" (paga), the guilt-offering term "guilt offering" (asham), the ransom construction "a ransom in place of many" (lytron anti pollon), the "righteous on behalf of the unrighteous" (dikaios hyper adikon) contrast, and the "place of atonement" (hilasterion) and "means of atonement" (hilasmos) cultic terms at face value. On this reading the words plainly predicate one party bearing what belonged to another, in that party's place, which directly affirms the proposition.

Foregrounds the victory vocabulary, chiefly "triumph over" (thriambeuo) and the disarming of the powers in Colossians 2:15, and reads the cross primarily as conquest of hostile powers and liberation of captives. In its strongest form this reading is fully lexically grounded in its own texts: those texts use triumph and ransom-from-bondage language, not penal-bearing language. It complicates the proposition only by contesting whether substitution is the central model, not by denying that substitution words occur.

Foregrounds "writing pattern" (hypogrammos, 1 Peter 2:21) and the call to follow in his steps, reading the death primarily as a moral pattern that shapes the believer. In its strongest form it notes that the very chapter that says he bore our sins also calls his suffering an example, so the example function is genuinely in the text. It complicates by disputing centrality, but the bearing verbs and the "on behalf of" (hyper) and "in place of" (anti) constructions are not reducible to example language, so on the lexical level the exemplar reading adds to rather than replaces the bearing predication.

Accepts that the death is a sacrifice and a sin offering ("guilt offering" asham, "place of atonement" hilasterion, "means of atonement" hilasmos, "to offer up" anaphero) but reads these cultically as expiation or cleansing of sin rather than as the bearing of a transferred legal penalty. This reading still affirms vicarious substitution in the sense the proposition states (Christ in the place of sinners, dealing with their sin) while declining the specifically penal framing of how. The substitution and place-taking claim is common ground; only the mechanism is contested.

hermeneutics.notes: Every reading that engages the cited texts grants that substitution and sin-bearing vocabulary is present and pan-canonical (spread across the whole Bible). The genuine divergence among readers is over which model (substitution, victory, example, non-penal sacrifice) is central or exclusive, and over whether the bearing is specifically penal. The words supply all these patterns but do not rank them, which is the lexical source of the remaining divergence even though the bare proposition (a substitute in the place of sinners) is affirmed.

stem_audit.notes: The stem speaks of a substitute, bearing the penalty, and in their place. Substitute and in their place are descriptive of the lexical pattern ("in place of" (anti) in place of, the bearing verbs "bear" (nasa), "carry" (sabal), "caused to land on" (paga), "to offer up" (anaphero), the "ransom" (lytron), the "guilt offering" (asham), "on behalf of" (hyper)) and are not a denominational shibboleth. The single loaded word is penalty, which encodes the penal (legal punishment) mechanism that the non-penal sacrificial reading contests; the bare vicarious-substitution claim does not by itself require the penal framing. The clause the sins of His people names the beneficiaries, but the lexical case for substitution as such does not depend on the extent question.

lay_summary: Across the cited passages the same substitution vocabulary keeps recurring in both testaments. In Isaiah 53 the Hebrew verbs "bear" (nasa) and "carry" (sabal) take our sicknesses, our pains, and then our iniquities as their objects, with the Servant as the subject, and these verbs return at the end of the chapter: he bore the sin of many in verse 12, he shall bear their iniquities in verse 11. Verse 6 uses "caused to land on" (paga in the causative form, meaning to cause to do) with the LORD as subject, he causes the iniquity of us all to land on the Servant, and verse 10 calls his life a "guilt offering" (asham), the technical word for the guilt offering that fills Leviticus 5 to 7. The first-person plural endings (the 'our' endings) throughout keep the speakers as the source of the burden and the Servant as the one carrying it, so the grammar predicates transfer, not parallel suffering. The New Testament reuses this engine. Jesus says he gives his life a "ransom in place of many" (lytron anti pollon), where the little word "in place of" (anti) means in place of or instead of in most of its uses, the strongest single word for substitution. First Peter says the "righteous one" (dikaios) suffered for the "unrighteous" (adikoi), and uses the offering-up verb "to offer up" (anaphero) with our sins on the tree, then by his wound you were healed. Second Corinthians says the sinless one was made "sin" (hamartia) on our behalf so that we might become the "righteousness" (dikaiosyne) of God in him, a two-way exchange. Romans calls Christ the "place of atonement" (hilasterion, the mercy seat) in his own blood, and First John calls him the "means of atonement" (hilasmos) by which our sins are dealt with. The pattern is dense, repeated, and spread across law, prophets, gospels, and letters, which is why the bare claim that Christ stood in the place of sinners lands firmly. Readers still diverge because the same texts also call the cross a victory over the powers and an example to follow, and because sacrifice words can be read as covering sin rather than as bearing a legal penalty. The words supply all these pictures but do not rank them, so the disagreement is over which picture is central, not over whether substitution language is there.
